title: Demystifying Information Flow Downgrading using the Real--Ideal Paradigm
summary: The real--ideal paradigm, an approach to security specification developed in the cryptography community, has the benefit that it can express sophisticated confidentiality and integrity requirements, even for decentralized systems. We show that this paradigm is the basis for a powerful and intuitive new semantic framework for language-based security. Our new framework cleanly and extensionally captures existing security definitions, including not only noninterference but also less understood information flow properties that involve downgrading, such as robust declassification and nonmalleable information flow. Past semantics for these properties have relied on intensional downgrading events. Further, we show that all of these properties can be enforced by a practical information-flow type system for a while-language that supports downgrading. Surprisingly, correctness of this type system is also characterized as a real--ideal simulation, with an important implication: the security of heterogeneous, decentralized systems with a strong (real) attacker can be understood by reasoning about a weak (ideal) attacker whose power is restricted to interaction with downgrading. This result explains the usefulness of nonmalleable information flow and related security properties. The results are fully formalized using the Rocq prover and are publicly available.

title: TauLang: A Language and Compiler for Space-Time Programming on Statically Scheduled Accelerators
summary: Statically scheduled accelerators such as Groq's Tensor Streaming Processor (TSP) achieve low-latency large language model inference by stripping dynamic synchronization hardware from the chip. With no caches, arbiters, or hardware schedulers, the compiler must fix the exact slice and issue cycle of every operation, so when an operation runs is a condition for correctness. Existing kernel languages cannot target such machines because they rely on hardware to resolve cycle timing and instead encode schedules implicitly in code structure. We present TauLang, a kernel language and compiler that makes time a first-class citizen of the program. The programmer schedules operations, loops, and composed kernels with parameterized explicit times, so exploring schedules means changing parameter values rather than rewriting code. TauLang validates explicit times algebraically in TauIR, its timed intermediate representation. It then solves tensor placement and cycle scheduling jointly in an integer linear program, using explicit times to group connected operations into timing clusters that prune the search space. On a cycleaccurate model of a TSP-like machine, joint search achieves a $1.40\times$ latency speedup across ten kernels over a space-first flow. A few explicit time pins keep latency within one cycle of the untimed schedules and scale joint search to 1,636 GEMM blocks, whereas untimed search finds no schedule at 32.

title: Verified Implementation of the Next-gen Borrow Checking Algorithm for Rust via Abstract Interpretation
summary:
Borrow checking is a central mechanism for Rust to ensure temporal memory safety. Its correctness is based on the intuition that the Aliasing XOR Mutability discipline guarantees that programs without borrow errors inherently could not access invalid references (i.e., pointers). However, existing work on formalizing borrow checking treats it either as a component of type systems or as symbolic execution describing resource transfer. None provides a direct explanation of the correctness of borrow checking algorithms such as Non-Lexical Lifetimes (NLL) or Polonius in the official Rust compiler that function more like static pointer analysis.
  We take a first step toward solving this problem by formalizing Polonius, the next-generation borrow- checking algorithm for the Rust compiler, on a core subset of Rust. We prove its correctness by showing that any program accepted by Polonius does not access invalid references at runtime. The key observation is that, when borrow checking is performed lazily, Polonius could be treated as a forward abstract interpretation on abstract domains recording pointer aliasing (borrowing) relations. By providing a concrete semantics that formally describes the Aliasing XOR Mutability discipline, we prove the soundness of this abstract interpretation, from which we derive memory safety of checked programs. This formulation of Polonius is implemented and formally verified in the abstract interpretation framework of CompCert. The correctness proofs are generated by an agentic AI under human guidance using paper proofs as proof outline. To the best of our knowledge, this is the first comprehensive formalization and verification of a borrow checking algorithm as manifested in the Rust compiler.
